Over the past few days, a statement I made was featured all over the news (for example, here, here, here and here) including in a tweet which received more than a million views here. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on Fox & Friends: “I’ve not seen any evidence to suggest this is…anything other than an asteroid.” On the other hand, I argued a few hours later here on Fox News that this so-called “dark comet” 1998KY98 is more likely the lost soviet spacecraft Phobos 1.

This argument was based on the detailed quantitative analysis presented in two papers that I co-authored with Adam Hibberd and Adam Crawl, which were posted here and here. These papers received major scrutiny from the editors and referees of scientific journals as well as self-declared experts and influencers on social media. In reference to the pushback that the two papers received and the lack of references to our work in the subsequent scientific literature, I wrote to my co-authors: “Comet experts and referees can play games and a viable alternative interpretation of all existing data for now. But after the rendezvous of the Hayabusa 2 spacecraft by the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA) with 1998 KY26 in July 2031, these dogmatists will have to admit the truth. As the Vatican learned from the Galileo affair, knowing the truth cannot be avoided, only delayed.”

Needless to say, I was disappointed when this morning, JAXA announced here that they “decided to abandon its plan to reach asteroid 1998 KY26, the final destination of the Hayabusa 2 probe. The decision was made due to engine problems that significantly exceeded the design life, and the probe will now head to a different asteroid.”

JAXA reported this at a meeting of the Cabinet Office’s Space Policy Committee on Monday November 16, 2026. According to this new report, in mid-August the fourth of Hayabusa 2’s main engines malfunctioned. The spacecraft switched to a mode which uses the usable parts of two malfunctioning engines, but this resulted in a loss of thrust. Reaching 1998 KY26 in July 2031 requires a gravity assist maneuver near Earth but JAXA’s decision was to change the destination to a flyby near the asteroid 2015 BM510.

What is the probability that JAXA reached this decision less than a day after my media appearances about the possibility that 1998 KY26 might be Phobos 1?

The answer can be quantified. The malfunctioning of Hayabusa 2’s engines was known for more than three months. The random chance of a decision being made within less than a day after my public appearances is less than 1%. This strongly suggests a correlation between JAXA’s decision and my media appearances.

***

In my interviews, I was often asked by reporters: “What is the evidence for the association of the so-called “dark comet” 1998 KY26 with the spacecraft Phobos 1?” My answer was as follows.

First, the orbit of 1998 KY26 is very close to that of the Russian probe Phobos 1, which suffered a failure 2 months after the launch in July 1988, due to upload of a faulty command. The first paper I co-authored here shows that by matching the trajectories of Phobos 1 and 1998 KY26.

Second, 1998 KY26 exhibits a non-gravitational push away from the Sun with no detectable shedding of gas or dust, as expected from the rocket effect of a comet. Our second paper here explains this push as the result of the reflection of sunlight by the solar panels of Phobos 1. Remarkably, we found that the anomalous non-gravitational acceleration and the brightness variation of 1998 KY26 can both be explained by the reflection of sunlight from Phobos 1 with its solar panels.

Recent radar and optical observations of 1998 KY26 indicate an unusually rapid spin-rate with a period of 5.35 minutes which is much faster than a natural pile of rocks glued by ice can sustain. The observations also implied a diameter of order 10 meters, and a shiny surface which reflects 52% of the sunlight impinging on it, both facts that are consistent with expectations from the Phobos 1 spacecraft.

The insistence of comet experts on the hypothesis that 1998 KY26 is a dark comet and their refusal to acknowledge the competing hypothesis that it is a technological object rather than an iceberg, underline how dogmatic the scientific mainstream has become.

Last week, a new paper published here in the prestigious scientific journal Icarus, reported that all locations on the surface or in the interior of 1998 KY26 are too hot for a comet. The orbit-averaged temperatures significantly above the sublimation point of volatiles in vacuum. These results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice. On the other hand, the results are consistent with the interpretation that 1998 KY26 is the lost soviet spacecraft Phobos 1. Nevertheless, the authors of this paper ignored this possibility and chose not to cite the two papers that I co-authored on this subject here and here.

Just this morning, I was asked by Amanda Greenwood from Newsweek (in an interview published here before JAXA’s new announcement): “Do you expect JAXA’s planned Hayabusa 2 encounter in 2031 to provide a definitive answer?” My answer was as follows.

Comet experts believe that 1998 KY26 is an iceberg, and they want to visit it. As a result, the Japanese Space Agency JAXA plans to land the Hayabusa 2 spacecraft on this object in July 2031. My alternative prediction is that when they land on it and study the properties of what they regard to be a mysterious iceberg that has invisible gas coming from it, they will find out instead the label: “Made in the U.S.S.R.” on it.

But now, as a result of the new decision by JAXA, we might never know for sure if 1998 KY26 and Phobos 1 are the same. This might make some dogmatists happy because they will not be proven wrong, but it goes against the spirit of the scientific method. Alternative interpretations should be tested by experimental data. When there is concern that the mainstream view might be wrong, we should aim to obtain missing data rather than avoid it.

***

Dark comets are a proposed class of curious hybrids between comets and asteroids. These objects show significant non-gravitational accelerations, yet they exhibit absolutely no sign of cometary outgassing in the form of a coma or tail. The first recognized interstellar object, `Oumuamua, showed these features and was suggested to be a `dark comet’ in recent mainstream publications, such as here. However, based on its inferred flat shape (published here) and non-gravitational acceleration (published here), I argued 8 years ago here that `Oumuamua might be pushed by sunlight and is technological in origin. The dark comet categorization of `Oumuamua and similar solar system objects was the mainstream response to my nontraditional suggestion.

The stakes for `Oumuamua being technological in origin are much higher than for 1998 KY26, because its high speed cannot be of human origin. Realizing that 1998 KY26 is technological rather than a `dark comet’ would suggest that maybe comet experts should not be trusted and `Oumuamua is the first encounter of astronomers with alien technology.

As I said all along, Elon Musk is probably not the most accomplished space entrepreneur over the past 13.8 billion years. There are billions of homes similar to Earth in our cosmic street of the Milky-Way galaxy and it is unreasonable to suggest that there are no space agencies beyond Earth that could have given birth to `Oumuamua.
